lessons.title: Common Mistakes: Chasing Appreciation and Ignoring Yield

children.text: Most bad property investments in India are not bad luck. They follow a small set of predictable mistakes: trusting a headline yield, paying for a metro line that is still a press release, borrowing heavily against a 2.5% yield, or letting one city's flats swallow the family's entire net worth. You have already met every one of these mistakes somewhere in this course, usually with a number attached. This final lesson gathers them in one place, shows what each one costs, and gives you the fix. By the end, you will have a checklist that catches the ten most expensive errors before you sign anything.

body.text: Nearly every costly property mistake comes from the same root: treating appreciation as a promise and yield as an afterthought. Rent is what you can verify today. Appreciation is what you hope for. Decide on what you can verify, and let what you hope for be the bonus.

body.title: Where the ten mistakes happen in a property purchase

children.text: Part 1: Measuring the Wrong Thing
Trusting the headline yield.

The broker divides a rent that includes maintenance by the agreement value and calls it a yield. Fix: use signed rent excluding maintenance, divide by the all-in cost, then subtract vacancy and running costs to get net yield.
Measuring gains without time, costs, tax or inflation.
"It doubled" and "₹16 lakh profit" ignore how long it took and what it cost. Fix: calculate XIRR on every dated cash flow, then convert to an after-tax, real return.
Using asking prices as proof of appreciation.

Portal listings and average launch prices rise for reasons that have nothing to do with your flat's value. Fix: rely on registered transaction prices for comparable homes, and check RBI's House Price Index or NHB RESIDEX for the city trend.

children.text: Part 2: Chasing Appreciation
Paying for infrastructure that is only announced.

Prices often jump on the announcement, then stall for years through approvals and construction. Fix: check funding, land acquisition, tenders and the implementing agency's own completion date, and value operating infrastructure and rising rents far above promises.
Borrowing heavily against a low yield.

With a 2.5% net yield and an 8.5% loan at 75% LTV, a year of flat prices loses about 15.5% of your own money, and prices must rise about 6% a year just for the loan to add anything. Fix: calculate the break-even appreciation, stress-test a 2 point rate rise and a vacant year, and keep the EMI gap comfortable.
Treating an under-construction discount as free money.

Until possession, the flat earns no rent while your instalments sit idle, and every month of delay pushes the rent further away. Fix: check RERA registration and the developer's delivery record, and demand a discount large enough to pay for the wait and the risk.
Forgetting carrying costs on locked flats and plots.

Arvind's Indore plot showed an 80% gain in ten years, yet after buying costs, upkeep, brokerage and inflation, the real return was about zero. Fix: let the property earn rent where possible, and include every carrying cost in your XIRR.

children.text: This chart assumes the same ₹1.45 crore sale price in April 2026 whatever the delay, so it shows only the cost of lost rent. Real delays usually hurt more: buyers living in rented homes keep paying rent elsewhere, and a project with a reputation for delays often sells at a lower price.

body.label: RERA's protection for buyer money
body.context: Under the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, developers of registered projects must deposit 70% of the money collected from buyers into a separate account used for that project's construction and land costs. Always confirm a project's registration on your state's RERA portal.

body.text: Two schemes deserve special caution. Assured rental or guaranteed return schemes promise a fixed yield paid by the developer, not by a real tenant, and payments can stop when the promise period ends or cash runs short. Subvention schemes, where the developer pays your pre-EMI interest until possession, leave you legally responsible for the loan if the developer stops paying. Read the agreements, and assume any guarantee is already built into the price.

body.title: Spot the biggest risk
body.question: A developer offers a studio unit in a new commercial complex in Noida with "12% assured annual rental for three years, paid by us". What is the biggest concern?
options: 12% is too low compared with residential yields
The income comes from the developer rather than a real tenant, may stop, and is likely built into an inflated price
Commercial units cannot be rented in Noida
Assured rental income is tax-free, which makes it too good to be true
body.explanation: A guarantee from the seller is not rental income. If the developer can fund 12% a year, the unit's price has probably been marked up to cover it. When the three years end, the real market rent, and the real yield on what you paid, may be far lower, and there may be no tenant at all.

body.title: Before paying for a promise
body.textWithBlank: Before paying extra for "upcoming" infrastructure, check whether its benefit is already ___ in to today's price.
body.explanation: Much of an infrastructure project's impact can be priced in at announcement. If you pay for it now, you need the project to arrive on time and to add value beyond what the seller has already charged you for.

children.text: Part 3: Ignoring Yield, Tax and Fit
Maximising rent instead of income.

The highest rent from a shaky tenant, or an aggressive hike that pushes a good tenant out, often earns less than a slightly lower, reliable rent. Fix: compare expected rent after the probability of exits, and value tenant retention.
Ignoring tax until the sale.

Rent is taxed every year at your slab rate, and a property sold within 24 months is taxed at your slab rate too. In Chapter 4, tax cut an office's lead over a flat from 1.18 to 0.48 percentage points. Fix: compare options on after-tax XIRR, hold beyond 24 months where possible, and plan exemptions before selling.
Letting property swallow the portfolio.

RBI's Household Finance Committee estimated real estate at about 77% of the average Indian household's assets. A second low-yield flat in the same city adds risk, not diversification. Fix: count your own home as property exposure, and consider REITs and financial assets for the rest.

body.title: The cost of a greedy rent hike
body.prompt: A Thane flat is let at ₹30,000 a month to a reliable tenant. Option 1: raise the rent 5% to ₹31,500, and the tenant stays all year. Option 2: demand ₹34,500, the tenant leaves, the flat sits empty for two months, the new tenant's brokerage costs one month's new rent, and the owner pays ₹4,000 a month maintenance while it is empty. Over the next 12 months, how much more does Option 1 earn, in rupees?
body.explanation: Option 1: ₹31,500 × 12 = ₹3,78,000. Option 2: 10 months × ₹34,500 = ₹3,45,000, minus brokerage of ₹34,500 and vacant-month maintenance of ₹8,000 = ₹3,02,500. The modest hike earns ₹75,500 more, before counting repainting and the risk that the new tenant is less reliable.

Buys another flat in the same city

columns.label: The disciplined investor
points: Starts from signed rent and net yield
Measures XIRR after tax and inflation
Borrows only what survives a bad year
Pays for what is operating and verifiable
Compares options on after-tax returns from day one
Checks concentration before adding more property

body.title: Spot every mistake in this message
body.scenario: A friend, Siddharth, sends this on WhatsApp: "Book two under-construction 2BHKs in Hinjewadi Phase 3 at the pre-launch price of ₹65 lakh each. Pay just 10% now, the bank funds 90%, and the builder pays the pre-EMI until possession. The metro line being built there will double prices. After possession, rent will cover the EMI. Or we flip both in 18 months for a 30% profit. I have already booked three!"
body.prompt: List every mistake or risk in this plan, using what you have learned in this course. Where possible, put a number on it.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Loan limit: a loan on a ₹65 lakh flat falls in RBI's band capped at 80% LTV, so the maximum loan is about ₹52 lakh, not ₹58.5 lakh. Stamp duty and registration, around ₹4.5 lakh per flat, are also paid from your own money.
2. Subvention risk: if the developer stops paying pre-EMI, you are liable for the loan. Read the tripartite agreement carefully.
3. Under-construction risk: no rent until possession, and delays are common. Check RERA registration, the developer's delivery record and the project's escrow compliance.
4. "The metro will double prices": the line is not yet operating, part of its benefit may already be priced in, and doubling needs about 7.2% a year for ten years, or far more over a shorter period.
5. "Rent will cover the EMI": the EMI on ₹52 lakh at 8.5% for 20 years is about ₹45,100 a month. At an illustrative rent of ₹20,000 for a 2BHK there, rent covers less than half. With a yield near 3% and a loan near 8.5%, leverage is negative unless appreciation beats roughly 6% a year.
6. "Flip in 18 months for 30%": the gain would be short-term, taxed at your slab rate. Stamp duty, brokerage and any transfer charges eat a large share of the gain, some developers restrict transfers before possession, and resale in an area with lots of new supply is hard.
7. Concentration: two flats from one developer in one micro-market doubles your exposure to a single project and a single location.
8. Social proof: Siddharth booking three is not due diligence. The right questions are about net yield, break-even appreciation, bear-case outcomes and fit with your own finances.

body.title: The ten-mistake check before you sign
steps: Net yield calculated from signed rent, all-in cost, vacancy and running costs.
Returns measured as XIRR on all cash flows, then after tax and after inflation.
Appreciation judged from registered transactions and official indices, not listings.
Infrastructure valued only at its real stage: operating, under construction or merely announced.
Loan stress-tested for break-even appreciation, a 2 point rate rise and a vacant year.
Under-construction purchase checked on RERA, developer record, and a discount that pays for the wait.
Carrying costs counted for any property that will sit empty.
Tenant chosen for reliability and rent set for retention, not maximum headline rent.
After-tax returns compared, and the sale planned beyond 24 months with exemptions in mind.
Total property exposure, including your own home, checked for concentration.

cards.definition: Using gross rent on agreement value instead of net yield on all-in cost.
Quoting total gains without time, costs, tax or inflation.
Treating listing prices or average launch prices as real appreciation.
Paying for infrastructure that is only announced or already priced in.
Borrowing at a rate higher than the property's total return.
Ignoring lost rent and delay risk on under-construction purchases.
Forgetting that empty property still costs money every year.
Chasing the highest rent at the cost of tenant reliability and retention.
Ignoring tax on rent and short-term gains until it is too late to plan.
Letting property in one city dominate your net worth.

points: Measure honestly: net yield on all-in cost, XIRR on real cash flows, and after-tax, real returns.
Judge appreciation from registered transactions and official indices, never from listings or averages distorted by the mix of homes sold.
Pay only for infrastructure and growth you can verify, and treat guarantees and subvention schemes with caution.
Borrow only if the property's total return clearly beats your loan rate, and only what survives a bad year.
Protect income by choosing reliable tenants and keeping them, rather than chasing maximum rent.
Plan tax from day one: rent is taxed yearly at your slab, while long-term gains are taxed once at a lower rate.
Count your own home, avoid concentration, and match yield-first or growth-first to your life rather than to a brochure.

children.text: That completes the course. You can now split any property's return into rent and appreciation, measure each one honestly, test a price against its income, see through leverage and tax, and choose a strategy that fits your own goals. The next time a broker sends a WhatsApp pitch, run the ten-mistake check before you reply.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. The people, properties, schemes, rents, prices and returns shown are illustrative. RERA provisions, RBI lending norms and tax rules change and vary in application, so verify current rules with the relevant authority and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser, a chartered accountant or a property lawyer before making any decision.
